claim: Natural environments feature mixtures of odorants of diverse quantities, qualities and complexities.
source: Natural environments feature mixtures of odorants of diverse quantities, qualities and complexities.
evidence: This is a general statement about natural environments presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript, but draws on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) are the first layer in the sensory pathway and transmit the olfactory signal to higher regions of the brain.
source: Olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) are the first layer in the sensory pathway and transmit the olfactory signal to higher regions of the brain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the olfactory system architecture.

claim: The response of ORNs to mixtures is strongly non-additive, and exhibits antagonistic interactions among odorants.
source: Yet, the response of ORNs to mixtures is strongly non-additive, and exhibits antagonistic interactions among odorants.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results and theoretical analysis presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Antagonism leads to an effective 'normalization' of the ensemble ORN response.
source: We show how antagonism leads to an effective 'normalization' of the ensemble ORN response, that is, the distribution of responses of the ORN population induced by any mixture is largely independent of the number of components in the mixture.
evidence: This is a key finding demonstrated through mathematical modeling and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The distribution of responses of the ORN population induced by any mixture is largely independent of the number of components in the mixture.
source: We show how antagonism leads to an effective 'normalization' of the ensemble ORN response, that is, the distribution of responses of the ORN population induced by any mixture is largely independent of the number of components in the mixture.
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling results shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Normalization arises from a novel mechanism involving the distinct statistical properties of receptor binding and activation, without any recurrent neuronal circuitry.
source: This property arises from a novel mechanism involving the distinct statistical properties of receptor binding and activation, without any recurrent neuronal circuitry.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion derived from the mathematical model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Normalization allows the encoding model to outperform non-interacting models in odor discrimination tasks.
source: Normalization allows our encoding model to outperform non-interacting models in odor discrimination tasks, leads to experimentally testable predictions and explains several psychophysical experiments in humans.
evidence: This is demonstrated through computational experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: The antagonistic encoding model explains several psychophysical experiments in humans.
source: Normalization allows our encoding model to outperform non-interacting models in odor discrimination tasks, leads to experimentally testable predictions and explains several psychophysical experiments in humans.
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling results shown in Figure 6 that reproduce psychophysical phenomena.

claim: Inhibitory feedback plays a key role in the adaptive immune system for proper combination of rapidity, sensitivity and specificity.
source: Inhibitory feedback plays a key role in meeting the challenge of a proper combination of rapidity, sensitivity and specificity (François et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to François et al., 2013.

claim: Inhibitory interactions in the form of receptor antagonism have been observed in experiments with olfactory receptor neurons.
source: Inhibitory interactions in the form of receptor antagonism have indeed been observed in experiments with olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) (Oka et al., 2004; Takeuchi et al., 2009; Kurahashi et al., 1994), although it has not been quantified systematically.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Receptor antagonism in ORNs has not been quantified systematically.
source: Inhibitory interactions in the form of receptor antagonism have indeed been observed in experiments with olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) (Oka et al., 2004; Takeuchi et al., 2009; Kurahashi et al., 1994), although it has not been quantified systematically.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field based on the literature.

claim: The response of cells expressing the mOR-EG receptor is strongly suppressed when methyl isoeugenol is delivered together with the receptor's cognate ligand, eugenol, at equal concentrations.
source: For instance, the response of cells expressing the mOR-EG receptor is strongly suppressed when methyl isoeugenol is delivered together with the receptor's cognate ligand, eugenol, at equal concentrations (Oka et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from a cited study.

claim: Evidence of intensity suppression and overshadowing in the perception of odorant mixtures comes from psychophysical observations.
source: Further evidence of intensity suppression and overshadowing (i.e. when one odorant makes another indiscernible) in the perception of odorant mixtures comes from psychophysical observations (Lawless, 1997; Keller and Vosshall, 2004; Doty and Laing, 2015; Thomas-Danguin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to psychophysical studies.

claim: The importance of peripheral interactions in shaping mixture perception has been directly shown by electrophysiological and psychophysical measurements.
source: The importance of peripheral interactions in shaping mixture perception has been directly shown by electrophysiological and psychophysical measurements (Bell et al., 1987; Laing and Willcox, 1987; Chaput et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The functional role of inhibition at the ORN level remains unknown.
source: However, the functional role, if any, of inhibition at the ORN level remains unknown.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Each ORN expresses receptors of a particular type, which typically display broad sensitivities to different odorants.
source: Each ORN expresses receptors of a particular type, which typically display broad sensitivities to different odorants, whereas each odorant binds promiscuously to receptors of many types.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ORN receptor expression patterns.

claim: Each odorant binds promiscuously to receptors of many types.
source: Each ORN expresses receptors of a particular type, which typically display broad sensitivities to different odorants, whereas each odorant binds promiscuously to receptors of many types.
evidence: This is established knowledge about odorant-receptor interactions.

claim: The axons of ORNs of a common type converge onto glomeruli.
source: The axons of ORNs of a common type converge onto glomeruli, where the axon terminals form synaptic contacts with mitral and tufted (M/T) projection neurons leading to the cortex, as well as local periglomerular (PG) interneurons.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about the olfactory system.

claim: The activation of an individual glomerulus represents the activation of a single ORN type.
source: The activation of an individual glomerulus therefore represents the activation of a single ORN type.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the anatomical organization of the olfactory system.

claim: Previous computational models that examined discrimination tasks have assumed a linear summation model of mixture response at the ORN level.
source: Previous computational models that examined discrimination tasks have, for simplicity, assumed a linear summation model of mixture response at the ORN level (Hopfield, 1999; Koulakov et al., 2007; Zhang and Sharpee, 2016; Zwicker et al., 2016; Mathis et al., 2016; Grabska-Barwińska et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a characterization of prior work supported by multiple citations.

claim: Odorant-receptor interactions depend on two distinct features: the sensitivity to binding and the efficiency of activation after binding.
source: A key aspect of the model is that odorant-receptor interactions depend on two distinct features: the sensitivity to binding and the efficiency of activation after binding, respectively.
evidence: This is a key assumption of the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Competitive antagonism occurs when a component in a mixture that binds strongly activates the downstream transduction pathway less effectively compared to other components.
source: Competitive antagonism occurs when a component in a mixture that binds strongly, activates the downstream transduction pathway less effectively compared to other components.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the manuscript based on the model.

claim: The biophysical model successfully captures the strongly non-linear peak response for different concentrations of the odorant.
source: For single odorants, the model successfully captures the strongly non-linear peak response for different concentrations of the odorant, the latency in response (Rospars et al., 2003), the quadratic rate of cAMP production (Takeuchi and Kurahashi, 2017), and calcium-based adaptation (Kurahashi and Menini, 1997) (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model results shown in Figure 1 and compared to cited experimental observations.

claim: The biophysical model successfully captures the latency in response.
source: For single odorants, the model successfully captures the strongly non-linear peak response for different concentrations of the odorant, the latency in response (Rospars et al., 2003), the quadratic rate of cAMP production (Takeuchi and Kurahashi, 2017), and calcium-based adaptation (Kurahashi and Menini, 1997) (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model results shown in Figure 1E and compared to cited experimental observations.

claim: The biophysical model successfully captures the quadratic rate of cAMP production.
source: For single odorants, the model successfully captures the strongly non-linear peak response for different concentrations of the odorant, the latency in response (Rospars et al., 2003), the quadratic rate of cAMP production (Takeuchi and Kurahashi, 2017), and calcium-based adaptation (Kurahashi and Menini, 1997) (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model results and compared to cited experimental observations.

claim: The biophysical model successfully captures calcium-based adaptation.
source: For single odorants, the model successfully captures the strongly non-linear peak response for different concentrations of the odorant, the latency in response (Rospars et al., 2003), the quadratic rate of cAMP production (Takeuchi and Kurahashi, 2017), and calcium-based adaptation (Kurahashi and Menini, 1997) (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model results shown in Figure 1F-G and compared to cited experimental observations.

claim: Strong amplification by the ion channels renders the mixture response hyper-additive at concentrations close to the sensitivity threshold.
source: Strong amplification by the ion channels render the mixture response hyper-additive at concentrations close to the sensitivity threshold; at higher concentrations, as the receptors become saturated and the odorants compete for limited binding sites, the response turns hypo-additive.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model based on the biophysical mechanisms.

claim: At higher concentrations, as the receptors become saturated and the odorants compete for limited binding sites, the response turns hypo-additive.
source: Strong amplification by the ion channels render the mixture response hyper-additive at concentrations close to the sensitivity threshold; at higher concentrations, as the receptors become saturated and the odorants compete for limited binding sites, the response turns hypo-additive.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model based on the biophysical mechanisms.

claim: The responses of the same ORN to saturating concentrations of different odorants yield very different firing rates.
source: Our assumption is motivated by observations made from spike recordings of single rat ORNs to odorant mixtures, where the responses of the same ORN to saturating concentrations of different odorants yield very different firing rates (Rospars et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from a cited study.

claim: The minimum latency of spiking response to different odorants at saturating concentrations can range from a few hundred milliseconds to a few seconds depending on the odorant-ORN pair.
source: Further evidence comes from examining the minimum latency of spiking response to different odorants at saturating concentrations (Figure 1E), which can range from a few hundred milliseconds to a few seconds depending on the odorant-ORN pair (Rospars et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by model results in Figure 1E and cited experimental observations.

claim: The lifetime of odorants bound to a receptor is short (of a few milliseconds).
source: The lifetime of odorants bound to a receptor is short (of a few milliseconds) and the probability of activation of a particular G-protein in a 50 ms interval at saturating concentrations is low (Bhandawat et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from a cited study.

claim: The probability of activation of a particular G-protein in a 50 ms interval at saturating concentrations is low.
source: The lifetime of odorants bound to a receptor is short (of a few milliseconds) and the probability of activation of a particular G-protein in a 50 ms interval at saturating concentrations is low (Bhandawat et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from a cited study.

claim: A purely competitive model of mixture interactions captured many cases from previous experiments on ORN mixture responses, but a significant fraction showed discrepancies.
source: While a purely competitive model of mixture interactions captured many cases from previous experiments on ORN mixture responses, a significant fraction showed discrepancies (Rospars et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an assessment of prior work based on a cited study.

claim: Non-competitive antagonistic effects, namely masking, can generate synergy or suppression.
source: Below, we show how non-competitive antagonistic effects, namely masking, can generate those effects.
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling results shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Masking is the phenomenon of non-specific suppression of CNG channel currents.
source: Masking is the phenomenon of non-specific suppression of CNG channel currents (Kurahashi et al., 1994; Takeuchi and Kurahashi, 2017).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Experimental evidence suggests that masking agents disrupt the lipid bilayer on the cell membrane, and thereby alter the binding affinity of cAMP to the CNG channels.
source: Experimental evidence suggests that masking agents disrupt the lipid bilayer on the cell membrane, and thereby alter the binding affinity of cAMP to the CNG channels (Takeuchi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from a cited study.

claim: The model reproduces qualitative features of odorant suppression observed in experiments.
source: The model above (and detailed in the Materials and methods) reproduces qualitative features of odorant suppression observed in experiments (Kurahashi et al., 1994; Takeuchi et al., 2013) (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing model results in Figure 2A-B to cited experimental observations.

claim: Both suppression and synergy are possible mixture interactions that could arise due to masking.
source: Importantly, we show that both suppression and, counterintuitively, synergy are possible mixture interactions that could arise due to masking (Figure 2C,D), both of which have been observed in experiments with single ORNs (Rospars et al., 2008).
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling results shown in Figure 2C-D and compared to cited experimental observations.

claim: Suppression and synergy have been observed in experiments with single ORNs.
source: Importantly, we show that both suppression and, counterintuitively, synergy are possible mixture interactions that could arise due to masking (Figure 2C,D), both of which have been observed in experiments with single ORNs (Rospars et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from a cited study.

claim: The response curve of the mixture, taking into account competitive binding alone, always lies between the response curves of the individual components.
source: This property is a simple consequence of the fact that the number of activated receptors for a mixture (at a particular total concentration) can never be larger/smaller than the most/least effective odorant delivered alone at the same total concentration.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the competitive binding mechanism.

claim: It is highly likely that only one component in the mixture occupies the receptors of ORNs of a particular type.
source: In other words, it is highly likely that only one component in the mixture occupies the receptors of ORNs of a particular type, and thus the response from these ORNs is determined by the activation efficacy of that specific component.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion derived from the mathematical analysis.

claim: The statistics of activation is conserved as the complexity of the mixture increases when ρ=0.
source: Since the entire distribution of activations across the ORN ensemble is invariant to the number of components in the mixture, we conclude that the statistics of activation is conserved as the complexity of the mixture increases, that is, the population response is 'normalized' (Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Normalization of the mixture response is a direct consequence of antagonism in receptor encoding, independent of any neural circuitry.
source: Remarkably, such a normalization of the mixture response is a direct consequence of antagonism in receptor encoding, independent of any neural circuitry.
evidence: This is a key theoretical conclusion of the manuscript.

claim: A sparse representation for a single odorant typically remains sparse for a complex mixture when ρ=0.
source: The upshot is that a sparse representation for a single odorant typically remains sparse for a complex mixture, allowing for improved performance in the detection of individual components (as quantified in the next Section).
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion supported by the normalization property.

claim: For experimentally observed levels (0.1–0.3) of sparsity, it is always advantageous to incorporate non-zero levels of antagonism into odorant encoding.
source: We find that for experimentally observed levels (0.1–0.3) of sparsity (Saito et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2006; Soucy et al., 2009; Vincis et al., 2012), it is always advantageous to incorporate non-zero levels of antagonism into odorant encoding (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling results shown in Figure 5B and compared to cited experimental observations of sparsity levels.

claim: Antagonism in receptors yields superior performance in component separation, independent of sparsity.
source: We find again that antagonism in receptors yields superior performance, independent of sparsity.
evidence: This is demonstrated through classification performance results shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: The combination of competitive antagonism and masking supports the diverse range of well-established psychophysical effects.
source: The upshot is that the combination of competitive antagonism and masking supports the diverse range of well-established psychophysical effects enumerated hereafter.
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Inhibition and synergy naturally arise from competitive antagonism.
source: Figure 6A further demonstrates that inhibition and synergy naturally arise from competitive antagonism.
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling results shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Stronger inhibition arises at higher concentrations as the glomeruli that are otherwise activated by an odorant when delivered alone are antagonized by the second odorant.
source: Stronger inhibition arises at higher concentrations as the glomeruli that are otherwise activated by an odorant when delivered alone are antagonized by the second odorant, leading to lower perceived intensity.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation derived from the model.

claim: At lower concentrations, competitive antagonism plays a limited role; instead, cooperative effects in the ORN transduction pathway result in hyper-additivity.
source: At lower concentrations, competitive antagonism plays a limited role; instead, cooperative effects in the ORN transduction pathway result in hyper-additivity, which pushes a few glomeruli above the activation threshold and gives rise to a small synergistic effect.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation derived from the model.

claim: Masking is readily explained by the model, where the inferred concentration is below the actual concentration as the masking agent's concentration increases.
source: Masking is also readily explained by our model, where the inferred concentration (based on the activated glomeruli) is below the actual concentration as the masking agent's concentration increases (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The reciprocal suppression of intense binary mixtures is conspicuously absent for a non-antagonistic model.
source: Figure 6C shows that the reciprocal suppression of intense binary mixtures is conspicuously absent for a non-antagonistic model.
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling results shown in Figure 6C.

claim: A strong asymmetric suppressive effect is observed when one of the odorants has a capacity for masking.
source: A strong asymmetric suppressive effect is observed when one of the odorants has a capacity for masking.
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling results shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Overshadowing for binary mixtures is intensified by antagonism.
source: Figure 6D demonstrates that overshadowing for binary mixtures is intensified by antagonism, in spite of its superior discriminatory performance for more complex mixtures.
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling results shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Normalization with increasing stimulus intensity or complexity is common in neural systems.
source: Normalization with increasing stimulus intensity or complexity is common in neural systems (Carandini and Heeger, 2011) and has been thought of as a circuit property that involves inhibitory synaptic interactions (Wachowiak et al., 2002; Cleland et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the Drosophila antennal lobe, activation of increasing number of receptors proportionally increases inhibition provided to any one glomerular channel.
source: In the olfactory system, this was elegantly demonstrated in the Drosophila antennal lobe, where activation of increasing number of receptors (or glomeruli) proportionally increases inhibition provided to any one glomerular channel (Olsen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from a cited study.

claim: In fish and mouse olfactory bulbs, increasing stimulus intensity is thought to recruit populations of interneurons that inhibit principal cells, leading to blunted activity for higher stimulus intensities.
source: Similarly, in fish and mouse olfactory bulbs, increasing stimulus intensity is thought to recruit populations of interneurons (namely, short axon cells) that inhibit principal cells, leading to blunted activity for higher stimulus intensities.
evidence: This is established knowledge about olfactory bulb circuitry.

claim: A mouse with a particular receptor forcibly expressed widely has remarkably similar activation of the mitral cell population despite the massive increase in the input when the cognate odorant is presented.
source: In an extreme example of this, a mouse with a particular receptor forcibly expressed widely has remarkably similar activation of the mitral cell population despite the massive increase in the input when the cognate odorant is presented (Roland et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from a cited study.

claim: Normalization is granted at the level of receptors by purely statistical reasons, without any additional circuit burden.
source: The key insight from our model is that normalization is granted at the level of receptors by purely statistical reasons, without any additional circuit burden.
evidence: This is a key theoretical conclusion of the manuscript.

claim: In the limit of full statistical decorrelation between ligands' binding affinity and activation efficacy, the distribution of activations across the ORN ensemble for a mixture coincides with that of a single monomolecular odorant.
source: In the limit of full statistical decorrelation between ligands' binding affinity and activation efficacy, the distribution of activations across the ORN ensemble for a mixture coincides with that of a single monomolecular odorant, a property which has been confirmed in the fly (Stevens, 2016).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction that is supported by a citation to experimental work in flies.

claim: Normalization at the first layer in the sensory pathway helps avoid early saturation effects that would confound the entire processing pathway.
source: Normalization at the first layer in the sensory pathway helps avoid early saturation effects that would confound the entire processing pathway.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion about the functional advantage of normalization.

claim: The perceived intensity level of an odorant is empirically related to the true concentration of the odorant as a power function.
source: Experiments show that the perceived intensity level of an odorant is empirically related to the true concentration of the odorant as a power function, reflecting their proportional relationship on a single logarithmic scale (Lawless, 1997; Wojcik and Sirotin, 2014).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from cited studies.

claim: The intensity level for binary mixtures perception is commonly described via a vector sum of the intensities of each component.
source: The intensity level for binary mixtures perception is commonly described via a vector sum of the intensities of each component (Berglund et al., 1973; Laing et al., 1984; Berglund and Olsson, 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited psychophysical studies.

claim: The vector model captures the level independent, symmetric nature of mixture suppression.
source: The vector model captures the level independent, symmetric nature of mixture suppression.
evidence: This is a characterization of the vector model from psychophysics.

claim: The biophysical model is consistent with an even broader range of perceptual phenomena, including level independency, synergy, symmetric and asymmetric suppression, masking and overshadowing.
source: The biophysical model presented here is consistent with an even broader range of perceptual phenomena, including level independency, synergy, symmetric and asymmetric suppression, masking and overshadowing.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the model's explanatory power, supported by the results in Figure 6.

claim: Global antagonistic interactions at the ORN level may play a major role in non-trivial perceptual phenomena.
source: The bottomline is that global antagonistic interactions at the ORN level may play a major role in non-trivial perceptual phenomena.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the modeling results.

claim: ORNs are far from simple relays, and their strong nonlinear interactions crucially affect olfactory processing.
source: In conclusion, ORNs are far from simple relays, and their strong nonlinear interactions crucially affect olfactory processing.
evidence: This is a concluding statement based on the modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The odorant receptor dynamics in the model is based on a two-step activation process analogous to previous works in vertebrates and the fly.
source: The odorant receptor dynamics in our model is based on a two-step activation process analogous to previous works in vertebrates (Rospars et al., 2008; Cruz and Lowe, 2013) and the fly (Nagel and Wilson, 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about the model's basis in prior work, supported by citations.

claim: A key aspect of two-step activation is that it separates sensitivity of ligand binding from activation efficacy.
source: A key aspect of two-step activation is that it separates sensitivity of ligand binding from activation efficacy (del Castillo and Katz, 1954).
evidence: This is a theoretical point supported by a citation to classic work.

claim: At the structural level, the distinction between binding and activation is consistent with observations on the binding and activation of GPCRs.
source: At the structural level, this distinction is consistent with observations on the binding and activation of GPCRs (Strange, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to work on GPCR structure and function.

claim: The explicit formulation of the pathway downstream of receptor activation allows going beyond pure competitive antagonism.
source: Moreover, this explicit formulation allows us to go beyond pure competitive antagonism, which was reported to explain about half the cases and thus requires generalizations (Rospars et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about the model's advantages, referencing limitations of prior work.

claim: Pure competitive antagonism was reported to explain about half the cases of mixture interactions.
source: Moreover, this explicit formulation allows us to go beyond pure competitive antagonism, which was reported to explain about half the cases and thus requires generalizations (Rospars et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an assessment of prior work from a cited study.

claim: Direct measurements from mammalian ORNs have been obtained in vitro in many biophysical studies studying signal transduction.
source: Direct measurements from mammalian ORNs have been obtained in vitro in many biophysical studies studying signal transduction (Lowe and Gold, 1995; Bhandawat et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement about experimental methods supported by citations.

claim: There is significant uncertainty about mimicking the native conditions in in vitro preparations in terms of delivery of odors and the ionic composition of the perfusion medium.
source: Although such preparations offer excellent access for measurement, there is significant uncertainty about mimicking the native conditions in terms of delivery of odors (airborne vs solution) as well as the ionic composition of the perfusion medium, which will affect response amplitudes.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of experimental limitations.

claim: Electrical recordings from individual ORNs are difficult and have low yield, but have offered tantalizing hints on different nonlinear interactions.
source: Electrical recordings from individual ORNs are difficult and have low yield, but have offered tantalizing hints on different nonlinear interactions (Rospars et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an assessment of experimental methods and their findings, supported by a citation.

claim: Glomerular imaging methods offer robust signals and extended recording times to obtain measurements at different concentrations and mixture ratios.
source: More extensive data will likely have to rely on glomerular imaging methods (Bozza et al., 2004; Rokni et al., 2014; Mathis et al., 2016), which offer robust signals and extended recording times to obtain measurements at different concentrations and mixture ratios (Soucy et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about experimental methods supported by citations.

claim: There are concerns about potential effects of feedback mediated by olfactory bulb neurons on ORN axon terminals, particularly through GABAb receptors.
source: Here too, there are some concerns including potential effects of feedback mediated by olfactory bulb neurons on ORN axon terminals, particularly through GABAb receptors (McGann et al., 2005; McGann, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about experimental confounds supported by citations.

claim: Carefully controlled experiments that isolate feedforward sensory signals could reveal the prevalence of antagonistic interactions in mammalian ORNs.
source: Carefully controlled experiments that isolate feedforward sensory signals could reveal the prevalence of antagonistic interactions in mammalian ORNs.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future experiments.

claim: If η and κ are highly correlated most of the time, then antagonistic interactions will likely have only weak impact on olfaction.
source: If these two parameters are highly correlated most of the time, then antagonistic interactions of the sort described in our theory will likely have only weak impact on olfaction.
evidence: This is a prediction about when the model's effects would be minimal.

claim: Even a modest decorrelation between η and κ will give rise to important effects on ensemble coding of odor mixtures even at the front end of the olfactory system.
source: Even a modest decorrelation, on the other hand, will give rise to important effects on ensemble coding of odor mixtures even at the front end of the olfactory system.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model's properties.

claim: Non-competitive antagonistic mechanisms, such as masking effects, have not been widely studied in mice.
source: Non-competitive antagonistic mechanisms, such as masking effects discussed here, have not been widely studied in mice and they may only occur for selected odorants.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of experimental work.

claim: Masking effects may only occur for selected odorants.
source: Non-competitive antagonistic mechanisms, such as masking effects discussed here, have not been widely studied in mice and they may only occur for selected odorants.
evidence: This is a speculation about the scope of masking effects.
